title: Richie Kamuca, appreciated too late
summary: Herman says musicians' estimates improve after death; Charlotte was drawn to Kamuca's haunting playing on the Las Vegas Herd album, and he valued his self-discipline.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Uh-huh. Let's see. Oh, you had a number of fine people -- you've already mentioned, who are no longer with us anymore that had been in your bands. There was another I just thought I'd ask you about, was Richie Kamuka.

What I've -- at least, what I've heard in the last year, there have been more comments about -- I really didn't appreciate him as much. And I've been listening to his recent records. I just heard that last night from somebody. said, I was in the same section, I didn't really know what -- he had all kinds of bad habits and things, but nevertheless, when he got down to business and he played, particularly a ballad, it was just pure something.
Yeah, well, I think this is something we
all live and die with, the fact that the estimates of your illustrious career come out much prettier when it's too late.
But I do feel, and I think one of the discerning people about Richie's playing is Charlotte.
She never understood a lot of my players, but one of the guys -- when they did a small-band thing, I did a.. album with the Las Vegas Herd, and I think he was on that, I'm sure he was.
Probably. He was on that. And she was intrigued with his approach to whatever piece we were playing.
A certain haunting (inaudible) and so on.
And then, of course, there were other things he did in the band and then he came back many times for short stays.

And he was always extremely -- musically and effective and good taste and once again, I have to use the word which I think answers a lot of things, that is discipline. He had a great deal of self-discipline, as far as his own playing was concerned.
